hotel-utility-supply-investment-due-dili.title: 酒店投资尽调：水、电、燃气供应要查清哪些问题？
hotel-utility-supply-investment-due-dili.titleEn: Water, Power and Gas Supply: Due Diligence for Hotel Investors
hotel-utility-supply-investment-due-dili.description: 从供水、供电及燃气的容量、可靠性、备用安排和增容成本，核查酒店经营计划能否实现，并将供应缺口纳入投资预算与交易条件。
hotel-utility-supply-investment-due-dili.descriptionEn: Assess water, power and gas capacity, reliability, backup arrangements and upgrade costs, then reflect verified supply gaps in the hotel investment budget and transaction terms.
hotel-utility-supply-investment-due-dili.author: 迈创兄弟C&T（MarvelBros C&T）
content: 一家酒店过去能正常营业，并不意味着它能够支撑下一位投资人的经营计划。增加客房、升级餐饮、延长营业时间，或者把燃气设备改为电力设备，都可能改变原有的供应需求。收购资料中的水电燃气账单，可以帮助了解过去的消耗和支出，却不能单独回答未来够不够用、供应是否可靠，以及接手后还要投入多少钱。
因此，水、电、燃气供应应当进入酒店投资尽调。投资人需要查清的，是拟定经营方案与物业实际供应条件之间有没有差距，差距能否弥补，费用与工期由谁承担，再据此判断投资预算、交付条件和开业安排是否成立。
在国际酒店语境中，这些通常归入公用设施供应。水与能源需要分别核算，又必须放在同一套经营逻辑中审视。全电酒店可以没有燃气，部分物业依赖区域供热或其他燃料，尽调应跟随实际供应方式，不要求每家酒店配置同样的系统。
从经营计划出发，才能问对问题
同样规模的酒店，有限服务与全服务经营的需求可能不同。国际金融公司2007年发布的旅游与酒店开发环境、健康和安全指南，将客房使用、清洁、洗衣、厨房、泳池及场地维护列为酒店用水场景，并指出建筑设计及运营方式会影响能源使用。它提供的是国际实践参考，具体适用仍需结合项目所在地和专业评估。
投资团队应先请未来运营方说明：哪些服务必须保留，哪些准备增加，客房与公共区域在什么时段同时使用，餐饮、洗衣和热水供应怎样安排。工程顾问据此核算需求，再与供应合同、接入条件和现场设备相互核对。只拿历史账单乘以预计入住率，容易漏掉服务方式变化带来的影响。
以一个假设情景说明：投资人计划把原本只提供早餐的酒店改为设有全天餐厅和宴会服务的物业。新增需求不只是多买几台厨房设备，还包括备餐、清洗、排风、热水及相关电力负荷。即使客房数量不变，也不能沿用原来的供应假设。
供水要查来源、质量和高峰承接
供水核查先弄清实际水源、供水责任方、允许使用的条件，以及日常供水和应急补水是否依赖同一来源。随后查看历史停供、低压及水质记录，再由专业人员核对储水、处理和楼内输配能力。酒店门口有供水管线，不能代替楼内使用端的验证。
这里需要把区域与物业分开。世界资源研究所的Aqueduct工具可以筛查地点面临的水压力、干旱和洪水等风险，但地图上的等级不是某家酒店的供水保证。投资人仍需向当地供应方和物业核实季节性限制、供水条件及可用替代方案。
高峰需求也不只是一天用了多少水。客人集中洗浴、早餐清洗与洗衣作业能否同时得到满足，应结合拟定运营时段检查；热水还需要核对加热与储存条件。污水排放和处理能力也应纳入相邻检查，避免只确认水能进来，却遗漏使用后的处理约束。
如果物业所在区域存在水资源压力，不能仅凭等级就否定项目；若确有可靠、合规且成本可承受的供应方案，仍应继续核实。反过来，区域总体风险较低，也不能掩盖物业自身的管网、储水或处理问题。
供电要区分用电量、峰值和可用容量
月度电量反映一段时间内用了多少电；某一时段同时运行的设备需要多大功率，则关系到峰值负荷。投资人不必亲自计算设备选型，但应要求工程顾问把合同允许的容量、接入设施能力、楼内配电条件与拟定负荷分开列明，解释哪里存在约束。
历史用电量较低，可能是效率较好，也可能是部分楼层没有开放、餐厅没有运营，或经营时段较短。应把账单与当时的入住、服务范围及设备运行记录一起看。若有分时用电数据，更有助于识别集中使用时段；没有数据，就把补测需求和不确定性写入尽调结论，不能以估计冒充已经确认的余量。
英国电网运营商UK Power Networks在商业物业增容说明中指出，项目费用和时间取决于具体工程，需要审查申请，有时还需现场勘查。这个例子不能给其他国家的酒店提供工期承诺，却提醒投资人：增容费用和完成日期必须取得针对本项目的依据。
因此，拟增加负荷的方案不能只留一笔笼统的工程预备费。需要确认供应方是否接受申请、现场要改什么、涉及哪些第三方条件，以及什么时候能够投入使用。关键条件未落实，就不应把新增服务按期营业当作确定收入。
燃气要查使用依赖，也要查替代路径
使用燃气的酒店，应先分清管道供应与储罐配送，再核对供应合同、实际使用范围、设备状态及相应检查记录。由合资格专业人员判断容量、压力、储存和安全条件是否适合计划用途。账单没有异常，不能替代这些核查。英国健康与安全执行局的餐饮及酒店燃气安全指南，也将专业检查与维护作为重要内容；其具体资格制度属于当地语境，其他市场应核对本地要求。
接下来要问的是：一旦供气受限，受影响的是厨房、生活热水、采暖，还是几项服务同时中断。运营方需要明确哪些服务必须继续，哪些可以临时调整，工程顾问再验证替代安排是否可行。
改用电力设备也要回到供电条件重新计算。假如厨房和热水都准备改为电力供应，不能只比较设备采购价和燃气费，还应核查新增电力负荷、配电改造及实际电价结构。燃气需求减少，并不代表总投入或供应风险必然下降。
对于全电酒店，燃气项注明不适用即可；使用区域供热、液化石油气或其他能源的物业，则沿其真实供应链核查。国际比较的价值，是识别不同供给条件，不是给每个项目套上同一种设备方案。
备用设施必须对应具体服务
“有水箱”“有发电机”还不足以说明酒店能维持怎样的服务。投资人应看到备用安排覆盖哪些负荷、能够持续多久、切换与维护记录是否完整，以及补给是否可获得。具体能力必须由工程核算和适当的验证支持，不能按设备名称判断。
还要检查系统之间的依赖。例如，储水能否送到使用端，需要核对相关泵及控制系统是否具有相应供电保障；依赖配送的备用燃料，也要核查运输受限时的补给条件。这些都是需要验证的情景，并非每家酒店都会遇到的既成事实。
康明斯发电机组应用手册区分了应急用途与用于避免经营损失的备用用途。相应地，法定应急保障与维持完整营业所需的能力，应分别列清。符合某项应急要求，不自动意味着所有客房、厨房和公共区域都能照常运转。投资人要知道供应受限时实际保留的是哪一部分经营能力，并让当地专业人员确认安全及合规边界。
把供应缺口转成投资条件
供应尽调最终应回到投资模型。日常费用需要按拟定运营方式重新估算，接入、增容、更新和备用设施的必要投入应单列，工期对开业或改造营业的影响也要说明。
美国能源部关于公用事业费率的资料，将用电量收费、需量收费及固定收费分别解释。它说明了为什么相同电量未必对应相同账单，但不是全球统一计价规则。评估任何物业，都应核对适用的实际合同和费率，确认历史优惠、固定期限价格或其他条件在交易后是否仍然适用。
测算时可以分别查看正常供应与一项有依据的中断情景。把备用运行费用、必要整改及可能影响的经营项目列出来，同时说明哪些有报价、哪些只是估计。没有证据，不给中断概率和损失金额填上看似精确的数字。
已确认且可以解决的缺口，可以进入预算、价格讨论或交付安排；关键供应能力、必要审批或工程期限仍无法确定时，应暂停依赖这些条件的投资承诺。资料缺失也不能直接写成设施存在缺陷，应先说明缺什么、由谁补、何时能够形成结论。
一页供应尽调表怎样使用
项目负责人可以把供水、供电和适用的燃气分别作为一行，每行填清六项内容：支持哪些经营服务，计划需要什么供应能力，现有能力由什么资料证明，有何缺口与备用安排，需要多少费用和时间，以及谁负责核实并形成结论。若一项服务依赖多种供应，在相关行中注明关联，避免各专业分别通过，组合起来却无法交付。
开始时，运营方给出拟定服务范围，卖方或开发方提供供应与设备资料，工程顾问核对能力和差距，财务人员把已核实费用放入测算。涉及合同延续、使用权或许可的问题，由当地相应专业人员核实。投资负责人应在约定的决策日前汇总未决项，不让资料清单与投资审批各走一条线。
这张表的完成标准，不是所有格子都有文字，而是关键服务有可追溯的需求依据，供应能力有相应证据，差距有可执行的解决路径，费用、期限和责任能够相互对应。不能确认的项目应保留为未决项，明确它会影响哪一项投资假设。
酒店的水、电、燃气供应，最终决定的是某些经营承诺能否兑现。投资人应在承诺资金之前，让运营计划与物业供应条件接受同一次核查；能补齐的缺口计入投入，不能确认的条件留在决策桌上，而不是留给接手后的团队。

contentEn: A hotel's ability to operate in the past does not necessarily mean it can support the next investor's business plan. Adding rooms, upgrading food and beverage services, extending operating hours or replacing gas equipment with electrical equipment may all change supply requirements. Water, electricity and gas bills in an acquisition data room can help explain past consumption and expenditure. On their own, however, they cannot establish whether future capacity will be sufficient, whether supply is reliable or how much additional investment will be needed after acquisition.

Water, power and gas supply therefore belong in hotel investment due diligence. Investors need to identify any gap between the proposed operating model and the property's actual supply conditions, establish whether it can be closed and determine who bears the cost and responsibility for delivery. Those findings should inform the investment budget, handover conditions and opening schedule.

In an international hotel context, these services are generally discussed as utilities. Water and energy need to be accounted for separately while being assessed within the same operating framework. An all-electric hotel may have no gas supply; other properties may rely on district heating or alternative fuels. Due diligence should follow the actual supply arrangements rather than assume that every hotel needs the same systems.
Start with the operating plan to ask the right questions

Hotels of similar size may have different requirements under limited-service and full-service operating models. The International Finance Corporation's 2007 Environmental, Health, and Safety Guidelines for Tourism and Hospitality Development identify guest use, housekeeping, laundry, cooking, pools and grounds maintenance as hotel water uses. They also note that building design and operating patterns influence energy use. The guidelines provide a reference for international practice; their application still requires consideration of the project's location and professional assessment.

The investment team should first ask the proposed operator to explain which services must be retained, which will be added, when guest rooms and public areas will be used simultaneously, and how food and beverage, laundry and hot water services will be organised. Engineering advisers can then assess demand and reconcile it with supply contracts, connection conditions and equipment on site. Simply multiplying historical bills by an occupancy forecast can miss the effects of changes in service delivery.

Consider a hypothetical example: an investor plans to reposition a hotel that serves breakfast only as a property offering all-day dining and banqueting. The additional requirements extend beyond purchasing kitchen equipment to food preparation, washing, ventilation, hot water and associated electrical loads. Even if the room count remains unchanged, the existing supply assumptions cannot simply be carried forward.
Water: check the source, quality and ability to meet peak demand

Water due diligence begins by establishing the actual source, the party responsible for supply, the conditions governing its use, and whether normal and emergency supplies depend on the same source. Review records of interruptions, low pressure and water quality, then have qualified specialists assess storage, treatment and distribution within the building. A water connection at the property boundary is no substitute for checking what reaches the points of use.

Regional conditions and property conditions need to be distinguished. The World Resources Institute's Aqueduct tools can screen locations for water stress, drought, floods and other water risks. A map classification is not a guarantee of supply to an individual hotel. Investors still need to verify seasonal restrictions, supply conditions and available alternatives with the local supplier and the property.

Peak demand involves more than the total volume used in a day. Whether concentrated guest showering, breakfast washing and laundry operations can be supported simultaneously should be assessed against the proposed operating schedule. Hot water also requires checks on heating and storage capacity. Wastewater discharge and treatment capacity should be reviewed alongside supply, so that confirming incoming water does not leave constraints on its subsequent disposal overlooked.

A property in a water-stressed area should not be rejected solely on the basis of that classification. A reliable, compliant and affordable supply arrangement may justify further investigation. Conversely, a low regional risk rating should not obscure problems with the property's own distribution, storage or treatment systems.
Power: distinguish consumption, peak demand and available capacity

Monthly electricity consumption measures how much electricity was used over a period. The power required by equipment operating at the same time determines peak demand. Investors do not need to size equipment themselves, but they should require engineering advisers to distinguish contracted capacity, connection capacity, the building's electrical distribution capability and the proposed load, explaining where constraints arise.

Low historical consumption may reflect good efficiency, but it may also reflect closed floors, an inactive restaurant or shorter operating hours. Bills should be considered alongside occupancy, the services provided and equipment operating records for the same period. Interval data, where available, can help identify periods of concentrated demand. If it is unavailable, further measurement requirements and uncertainty should be recorded in the due diligence findings. An estimate must not be presented as confirmed spare capacity.

In its guidance on increasing supply to commercial properties, UK Power Networks explains that project costs and timing depend on the work required, with applications subject to review and sometimes a site visit. This example provides no timetable for hotels in other countries. It does, however, illustrate why the cost and completion date of a capacity upgrade require evidence specific to the project.

A proposal that increases electrical load therefore needs more than a general engineering contingency. The team should establish whether the supplier will accept the application, what work is required on site, which third-party conditions apply and when the upgraded supply can be used. Until critical conditions are resolved, revenue from new services opening on schedule should not be treated as certain.
Gas: identify operational dependencies and assess alternatives

For hotels using gas, distinguish piped supply from deliveries to on-site tanks, then review the supply contract, actual uses, equipment condition and relevant inspection records. Appropriately qualified specialists should assess whether capacity, pressure, storage and safety conditions suit the proposed use. An unremarkable bill cannot replace those checks. The UK's Health and Safety Executive guidance for catering and hospitality also addresses professional inspection and maintenance. Its specific qualification requirements belong to that jurisdiction; requirements in other markets must be checked locally.

The next question is what would be affected by a restriction in gas supply: the kitchen, domestic hot water, space heating or several services at once. The operator should identify which services must continue and which can be temporarily adjusted. Engineering advisers can then establish whether the proposed alternatives are feasible.

Switching to electrical equipment requires a fresh assessment of the power supply. If both the kitchen and hot water systems are to be electrified, the comparison should extend beyond equipment purchase prices and gas bills to additional electrical loads, distribution upgrades and the applicable electricity tariff structure. Lower gas demand does not necessarily mean lower total investment or supply risk.

For an all-electric hotel, record gas as not applicable. Where a property uses district heating, liquefied petroleum gas or other energy sources, investigate its actual supply chain. International comparison is useful for identifying different supply conditions, not for prescribing the same equipment solution to every project.
Match backup arrangements to specific services

The presence of a water tank or generator does not establish which hotel services can be maintained. Investors should be shown the loads covered by backup arrangements, how long they can be supported, whether changeover and maintenance records are complete, and whether replenishment is available. Actual capability requires engineering calculations and appropriate verification; it cannot be inferred from the name of the equipment.

Dependencies between systems also need examination. Delivering stored water to the points of use, for example, requires checking the power provision for the relevant pumps and controls. Backup fuel that depends on deliveries requires an assessment of replenishment when transport is restricted. These are scenarios to investigate, not events assumed to have occurred at every hotel.

Cummins' generator application manual distinguishes emergency applications from standby applications intended to prevent business losses. Accordingly, the capacity required for statutory emergency provision and the capacity needed to maintain full hotel operations should be listed separately. Compliance with an emergency requirement does not automatically mean that all guest rooms, kitchens and public areas can operate normally. Investors need to understand which operating capabilities would actually remain available during a supply restriction, with local professionals confirming the safety and compliance boundaries.
Translate supply gaps into investment conditions

Supply due diligence should ultimately inform the investment model. Recurring costs need to be reassessed against the proposed operation, while necessary expenditure on connections, capacity upgrades, replacements and backup facilities should be identified separately. The effect of delivery times on opening or trading during refurbishment also needs to be explained.

The US Department of Energy's guidance on utility rate options distinguishes energy charges, demand charges and fixed charges. This helps explain why the same electricity consumption may not produce the same bill, but it is not a universal pricing framework. For any property, review the actual contracts and tariffs and establish whether historical discounts, fixed-term prices or other conditions will continue after the transaction.

The assessment can consider normal supply alongside a disruption scenario grounded in available evidence. Identify backup operating costs, necessary remedial work and the activities that could be affected, distinguishing quotations from estimates. Where evidence is lacking, do not assign apparently precise probabilities or loss figures to interruptions.

Confirmed gaps with feasible solutions can be reflected in budgets, price discussions or handover arrangements. Where critical supply capacity, necessary approvals or engineering delivery dates remain uncertain, commitments that depend on them should be deferred. Missing information is not proof of a defective facility. First specify what is missing, who will provide it and when a conclusion can be reached.
How to use a one-page supply due diligence worksheet

The project lead can create a separate row for water, power and, where applicable, gas, recording six items for each: the operating services supported; the capacity the plan requires; the evidence for existing capacity; gaps and backup arrangements; costs and timing; and the person responsible for verification and the resulting conclusion. Where a service depends on several supplies, note those connections in the relevant rows. This avoids separate disciplines approving their own elements without confirming that the combined system can deliver the service.

At the outset, the operator defines the proposed services, the seller or developer provides supply and equipment records, engineering advisers check capacity and gaps, and the finance team incorporates verified costs into the appraisal. Local specialists should examine questions about contract continuity, rights of use or permits. The investment lead should consolidate unresolved issues before the agreed decision date, keeping the document review connected to investment approval.

Completion is not a matter of filling every cell. Demand for critical services should have a traceable basis; supply capacity should have supporting evidence; gaps should have executable solutions; and costs, deadlines and responsibilities should align. Items that cannot be confirmed should remain open, with the investment assumptions they affect clearly identified.

A hotel's water, power and gas supply ultimately determine whether certain operating promises can be fulfilled. Before committing funds, investors should bring the operating plan and the property's supply conditions into the same review. Gaps that can be closed belong in the investment budget. Conditions that remain unconfirmed belong on the decision table, rather than being left for the team taking over the hotel.

World Resources Institute: Aqueduct, water-risk screening tools and their scope.

https://www.ukpowernetworks.co.uk/i-already-have-electricity-commercial/add-more-power/add-more-power-cost-time-and-whats-involved

US Department of Energy: Evaluating Your Utility Rate Options, explanations of energy, demand and fixed charges.
https://www.energy.gov/cmei/femp/evaluating-your-utility-rate-options

https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/cais23.pdf
